Lofos Kapi Before and After the Holocaust of Kalavryta

How a hillside above Kalavryta became a place of mass violence, mourning, and public remembrance — and how its landscape has continued to change.

Eleni Gouvelou · Panagiota Katsaramenidou

A photographic history of place

When a landscape becomes a witness

On 13 December 1943, German occupation forces carried out the massacre of male civilians at Kapi Hill, overlooking Kalavryta. In the decades that followed, the hill was gradually remade as a place of burial, remembrance and public commemoration.

Drawing on archival photographs, site history and contemporary views, this essay follows the transformation of a once-ordinary hillside into a landscape marked by absence and collective memory.

Content note: This exhibition discusses a mass execution of civilians and its aftermath. The photographs shown here document Kalavryta and the memorial landscape; they do not depict the act of killing.

Orientation

The hill above Kalavryta

Kapi Hill stands above Kalavryta, a town in Achaea in the northern Peloponnese. Local names for the location have included Kapis’ Field and Kapis’ Hill. These maps locate the town and the memorial site; they are orientation aids, not evidence of the events of 1943.

CHAPTER 01

Before the rupture

A town beneath the hills

From April 1941 to October 1944, Greece lived under Axis occupation. German forces carried out widespread reprisals, destruction and executions of civilians. Kalavryta and the surrounding villages of Achaea suffered one of the occupation’s most devastating episodes.

In November 1943, the commander of the German 117th Jäger Division, Karl von Le Suire, planned an operation against the resistance in the Kalavryta region. The German command later presented the destruction of the town as retaliation for the killing of captured German soldiers. As the contributors note from Lazaris’s archival study, the operation had already been planned before those prisoners were killed on 7 December 1943.

In this first photograph, Kalavryta appears as a town within its surrounding hills. The image cannot tell us what its inhabitants were thinking or anticipating. It preserves the landscape that would soon become inseparable from the events of December 1943.

CHAPTER 02

The massacre and its aftermath

13 December 1943

On 13 December 1943, German occupation troops led male residents of Kalavryta to Kapi Hill and executed them. The town was set on fire. Women and children had been confined in the school building; they escaped the burning building. The massacre is remembered as one of the most severe mass crimes committed against civilians in occupied Greece.

The two photographs below show Kalavryta after the catastrophe. They record the town and the nearby slope, but also invite a more difficult question: what can a photograph of a damaged place convey about the people who are no longer visible?

CHAPTER 03

The first transformations

From Kapis’ Field to a site of memory

Before the massacre, the hill was known locally as a field or hollow associated with the landowner Kapis (or Kappis). After the execution, families buried relatives there and began to mark the ground with graves and crosses. A place in the landscape became a place that people returned to in mourning.

Gradually, the execution site was delineated and reshaped. The cross at the summit introduced a visible marker that could be seen from below, while the process of marking the hillside made remembrance part of the town’s everyday geography.

CHAPTER 04

Monument and symbolism

Giving grief a form

The memorial did not acquire its present appearance all at once. The contributors trace successive additions across the post-war decades: the large cross, Anna Vafia’s sculpture of the Petrified Mother, and a monumental ensemble shaped by the work of Ilias Skroumbelos, Christos Iakovidis and Giannis Liapis.

The sculpted mother evokes the grief of families who lost loved ones, and also the labour of the women who helped rebuild Kalavryta after its destruction. The memorial’s concrete slabs carry names and ages; their spatial arrangement is interpreted in the contributors’ essay as a reminder of the encirclement experienced by the townspeople.

Memorial light offerings and burial markers show how the design of the site brings together civic remembrance, local ritual and individual mourning.

1959

Cross erected at the hilltop, according to the submitted chronology.

1960

The Petrified Mother sculpture, as dated in the submission.

1970s

Later arrangement of the monument, as described in the submitted essay.

These dates reflect the authors’ account; published descriptions differ on dates of design, installation and subsequent alterations.

The Petrified MotherAnna Vafia’s sculpture introduces a human form into a landscape otherwise marked by names, walls and crosses. The artist’s figure has become one of the site’s enduring symbols of grief, care and survival.
CHAPTER 05

Architecture of public memory

An enduring landscape

The memorial’s mature layout brings the hilltop cross into conversation with the lower commemorative space. Slabs of different heights, the names of the executed, a cenotaph and the slope itself form a sequence that visitors encounter while ascending the site.

In 1993, the Greek state designated the Site of Sacrifice a protected historic site, acknowledging the hill’s significance not only for the people of Kalavryta but also for the memory of the country as a whole. The official designation, published in Government Gazette 348/B on 17 May 1993, recognises the landscape as a place of historical significance.

Photographs of the developed memorial and today’s landscape show continuity, but also the extent to which remembrance is made through physical interventions: paths, walls, planting, monuments and the care given to the site.

The landscape is part of the evidence

In this photo essay, the hill is not simply a backdrop for a historical event. Its paths, memorial elements and visibility from the town show how remembrance becomes something encountered, maintained and revisited.

CHAPTER 06

Memory in public practice

The annual return

Every year, commemorations in Kalavryta culminate on 13 December. According to the contributors’ account, the principal ceremony begins with a memorial service at the Metropolitan Church. Participants then move through the town towards the Municipal Museum of the Kalavrytan Holocaust and continue along the route to the Execution Site.

At the hill, wreaths are laid and the names of the executed are read aloud. This procession carries memory beyond a fixed monument: the commemorative path allows the town’s residents and visitors to encounter places associated with what happened in 1943.

For Gouvelou and Katsaramenidou, the hill’s transformation raises a central public-history question: how does a massacre reshape both local memory and the landscape through which a community remembers?

Closing reflection

A place that calls people back

The landscape of Kapi Hill holds more than the memory of a single day. Its development as a memorial and the recurring acts of commemoration show how a community continues to give public form to grief, testimony and the responsibility to remember.

Curatorial note

Terminology. The project retains the authors’ title, which uses the established local expression “Holocaust of Kalavryta.” In describing the specific event of 13 December 1943, the exhibition also uses “Kalavryta massacre,” distinguishing this crime from the Holocaust of European Jewry.

Chronology and evidence. The contributor’s bibliography includes a Government Gazette reference dated 7 December 1936 describing remembrance of victims of the German Occupation. This cannot be chronologically correct; the original document and its date require verification. The exhibition does not use that entry to establish post-war memorial chronology. Similarly, exact dates for the memorial’s design, construction and later alterations differ between accounts; the dates above are explicitly identified as those supplied in the authors’ essay.

Photographic sources. The historical photographs provide evidence of changing place and commemorative structures. They should not be interpreted as direct images of the executions or as proof of the experiences of people not individually identified in them.
